## Definition

The **Mann-Whitney U test** (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is a non-parametric test that compares the distributions of two independent groups. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other.

## When to Use

Use a Mann-Whitney U test when:

- Comparing two independent groups
- Data are ordinal, or continuous but non-normal
- Sample sizes are small
- Outliers are present
- Assumptions of the independent t-test are violated

## How It Works

1. Combine all observations from both groups
2. Rank all values from lowest to highest
3. Sum the ranks for each group
4. Compare rank sums to expected values

## The Test Statistic

$$U = n_1 n_2 + \frac{n_1(n_1 + 1)}{2} - R_1$$

Where:

- $n_1, n_2$ = sample sizes of groups
- $R_1$ = sum of ranks in group 1

## Assumptions

| Assumption | Notes |
|------------|-------|
| Independence | Observations between groups independent |
| Ordinal data | At minimum, can rank the values |
| Similar shape | Distributions have similar shape |

## Effect Size

Calculate **rank-biserial correlation** ($r$):

$$r = \frac{2U}{n_1 n_2} - 1$$

| r value | Interpretation |
|---------|----------------|
| 0.1 | Small effect |
| 0.3 | Medium effect |
| 0.5 | Large effect |

## R Code Example

```r
# Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum)
wilcox.test(score ~ group, data = mydata)

# With exact p-value for small samples
wilcox.test(score ~ group, data = mydata, exact = TRUE)

# Effect size
library(effectsize)
rank_biserial(score ~ group, data = mydata)
```

## Reporting (APA Style)

> A Mann-Whitney U test indicated that scores were significantly higher in Group A (*Mdn* = 75) than Group B (*Mdn* = 68), *U* = 245, *p* = .023, *r* = .34.

Note: Report medians rather than means for non-parametric tests.

## Comparison with Independent t-test

| Feature | Independent t-test | Mann-Whitney U |
|---------|-------------------|----------------|
| Data type | Continuous, normal | Ordinal or non-normal |
| Central tendency | Compares means | Compares distributions |
| Assumptions | More restrictive | Fewer assumptions |
| Power | Higher when assumptions met | Lower but more robust |
